name: Linear gauntlet
structure: One long journey from one edge of the map to the opposite edge along a valley, canyon, road, causeway or ridge. Zones follow one another in a line with bends, but the route never doubles back and there is no central lake, chasm or void.

name: Hub and wings
structure: The Arrival leads to a central hub plaza near the middle of the map, dense with buildings and monuments (never water). Three wings branch off the hub, each ending in a boss zone; the finale lies behind a sealed gate off the hub that opens once the wings are cleared.

name: Switchback ascent
structure: The route zigzags up one long slope or mountain face in 4–6 switchbacks, each turn a terrace zone, cliffs and retaining walls between them. The finale is at the top, on the far edge from the start.

name: Inward spiral
structure: The route spirals inward and upward from the outer edge toward a raised centre where the finale stands: a hill, citadel, great tree or tower — never water. Each turn of the spiral is higher than the last.

name: Descent into a pit
structure: A great quarry, crater, stepwell or sinkhole fills much of the map; the route descends its terraced sides to the floor, where the finale is. The pit floor is solid ground (or a lava lake with an island, for volcanic settings).

name: Island hopping
structure: Separate landmasses (islands, pinnacles or floes) in water, lava, mist or a deep drop, linked by bridges, causeways, rope walkways and boats. Each island is a zone, built up and dressed. The gaps may cover up to half of the map.

name: Fork and rejoin
structure: Soon after the start the route splits into two different paths — a high road and a low road, or two wings with different characters — each with its own zone and boss, rejoining before the finale. The two paths look and feel different.

name: Layered siege
structure: Entered from one edge: a siege camp outside, then an outer wall with a gatehouse, a dense lower town or bailey, an inner wall, and the keep or citadel on the far side. The walls cross the whole map.

name: Labyrinth
structure: Dense walls, hedges, ruins, pillars or rock fins form a maze across the map with two or three alternative routes between zones and dead-end pockets holding rewards. The finale is at the maze's heart or far side.

name: Two loops
structure: Two loops of route share a central crossing plaza: the first loop is cleared to unlock the second, which leads to the finale. The loops wind through built-up ground and terrain, not round a lake.

name: Ridge and spurs
structure: A long ridge, causeway or colossal bridge forms a spine across the map; zones sit on spurs and terraces off both sides of the spine, and the finale is at the spine's far end.

name: River crossings
structure: A narrow river (10–30 m wide; lava or a dry bed in some settings) winds across the whole map; the route crosses it back and forth by bridges, fords and ferries, with zones on alternate banks. The river never widens into a lake that fills the map.

name: Ruined city blocks
structure: A dense ruined town or city: streets, alleys, squares and courtyards between many buildings. Zones are squares, courtyards, gardens and great halls open to the sky. Buildings fill most of the map.

name: Open battlefield
structure: A wide open plain, dune field, ice sheet or plateau with scattered landmarks — ruins, siege engines, camps, wrecks, a fallen colossus. Zones are areas of the field around landmarks rather than walled courts; paths are loose; the edges are cliffs, walls or drops.

name: Loop round a landmark
structure: The route circles a central landmark — a lake, chasm, mound or great monument — and comes back near the start.
